data.title: The Blank Beside It
data.text:
I am Mara Vey. I kept Tomas Lind’s papers, and I have put his 1998 notebook beside his last letter. Above the stakes at Kessel, he writes that a lake has appeared, grey-green and filling. You took his field cabin in an earlier valley. Here, Tomas Lind’s chalet is intact; the question of the kettles has survived the journey better than most correspondence.

The Upper Vell dam held for ten summers, then came down. The village went by the green route Anna had drawn and they had practised. Riverside’s council deferred Sorel’s spillway twice. Gil Harrow wrote that the inspectors called the dam satisfactory, the harbour needed dredging, the school roof leaked, and he believed there was time. The flood levy fell short; on one spoilt paper, someone wrote, “I would if I could.” Some households were already stretched. The cost did not fall evenly, though the water found its way through all the plans.

Tomas asks for a new stake line, higher up, where the ice remains. Whether someone will take up that work is still open. I leave a clean page beside his letter.

issues: “You took his field cabin” implies an act not supported by the history; the earlier chapter records Lind’s field cabin as destroyed.

“The question of the kettles has survived the journey better than most correspondence” asserts that most correspondence did not survive; the letter supports the joke about the kettles, but not that comparison.
“The flood levy fell short” could suggest a funding shortfall; the record says the town voted down the yearly levy.
“The water found its way through all the plans” implies every plan failed, but the record says the village used its practised green route. Avoid the claim that all plans failed.

The middle paragraph reads as a report-like inventory of the dam, route, council decisions, Harrow’s letter, and levy. Recast it as a reflection rooted in those records rather than a sequence of summaries.

“His field cabin was destroyed in an earlier valley” gives the cabin a location not supported by the record, which identifies it as the cabin above the third falls; say it was destroyed in the earlier chapter instead.
“I have put his 1998 notebook beside his last letter” calls the October 2039 letter his last without evidence that it was his final letter; refer to it as Tomas’s letter instead.
“The green route Anna drew” misattributes the route: Anna drew the route the lake came down, while the village took the separate green route they had practised.
“Whether someone will take up that work is still open” asserts an unresolved future outcome not established by the letter; keep to what the letter says about drilling a new stake line.

“Gil Harrow set down why the spillway was deferred twice” treats all his listed reasons as true. His letter gave them as his account, but the inspectors’ assessment was not a true reason for the 2009 deferral; attribute the account to him and preserve that distinction.
